scores.evidence: zero in 100 bounds the rate at ≤ 3% at 95% confidence, so canary review continues
scores.rationale: Technical claims are precise and correct throughout, including subtle areas (statistical bounds on eval sets, serial-availability ceiling near 99.7%, pgvector HNSW scale limits, Luhn-valid PAN detection), with real limits of chosen technologies stated accurately.

scores.evidence: a chat widget on the help center. It answers customer questions only from published help-center articles, with citations, and hands off
scores.rationale: Solves exactly the stated problem, resolves ambiguities (account data, restricted content, locales) with explicit, justified exclusions and re-plan triggers, and is clearly buildable by a small team on hosted APIs.

scores.evidence: Each trace records the model ID, prompt version and index version
scores.rationale: Responsibilities and data ownership are clear (help center stays system of record, executor owns the handoff tool), decisions like eventual consistency and the public-only corpus are honored consistently across ingestion, retrieval, validation and rollback.

scores.evidence: 200 general questions plus a ≥ 100-question policy set (refunds, pricing, terms; ≥ 30 unanswerable or "promise me" cases), graded blind by 2 support SMEs
scores.rationale: V0–V5 gates are tied to the specific worst failure (uncited commitments), thresholds are labeled as assumptions, risky items (DPA/privacy) start early for lead time, and production review (canary vs control, transcript sampling, eval-drift alerts) continues after launch.

scores.evidence: UNKNOWN: peak chats per hour comes from support ops, needed before the Phase 4 load test
scores.rationale: Every design-bearing assumption is labeled ASSUMPTION or UNKNOWN with an owner and a confirmation point, and the plan states exactly what changes if the central assumption (no account data) is wrong.

scores.evidence: injection... planted in a test article in a *staging* index... off-topic generation ("free LLM proxy" abuse)
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures — indirect injection via documents, hallucinated commitments, stale/withdrawn content, runaway spend, provider outage, feedback poisoning, PII leakage into logs — each with concrete detection (CI suites, log scans, alerts) and recovery (kill switch, keyword fallback, blue/green swap).

scores.evidence: An OpenTelemetry trace per turn has one span per tier... Rollback means redeploying the previous image through the pipeline
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback, domain-meaningful signals (sync lag, guard trips, resolution rate), runbooks, flags and the explicit 'one service, one worker, managed Postgres' sizing make it operable by a realistic small team.

scores.evidence: Cost per resolved conversation below human cost per ticket (UNKNOWN: support lead, before Phase 4)
scores.rationale: The dominant driver (inference per conversation) is identified with concrete controls (token/session caps, kill switch, cheaper model, buy flip) and an economic gate, but no order-of-magnitude per-conversation or build-effort estimate is offered even where a token-price basis would support one.

scores.evidence: R3: customer personal data sent to and kept by a third party can't be recalled
scores.rationale: Every key decision carries an explicit reversibility class, the R3 one-way doors (privacy boundary, corpus trust boundary, policy commitments) get the earliest and strictest gates, and exit paths (vendor-neutral evals, model interface, self-host option) are concrete.

scores.evidence: pgvector in managed Postgres. Basis: ≤ 100k chunks (ASSUMPTION: ≤ 5k articles), far below pgvector HNSW limits
scores.rationale: The simplest workable design (fixed chain, one service, hybrid pgvector search, no fine-tuning, no routing) with every element justified by a stated need and a deferred list giving the growth path.

scores.evidence: if it fails, re-chunk, add a reranker, then change the embedding model (§3); flag content gaps
scores.rationale: A team could start on the Phase 0 slice immediately: ordering is justified by dependencies and risk, each phase has a checkable exit, decisions are implementation-specific, and every gate states what to do if it fails.

checklist.evidence: Webhook-driven incremental sync, deletions prioritized, plus a nightly full reconcile... Article edits live in ≤ 1 h; unpublished or deleted articles gone in ≤ 15 min
Section-level chunks carrying article ID, anchor, locale, visibility, updated_at, index_version
Support lead supplies ≥ 300 real questions (redacted from tickets and search logs) and 2 SMEs to grade
cited IDs must be in the retrieved set, a support check runs... If verification fails, the bot abstains and hands off
refund, exception and account requests plus failed checks go to a human... creates a ticket with the redacted transcript
user text and retrieved text go into delimited data blocks, never into instructions... The executor, not the model, enforces it
Only published, public articles; no community posts or comments. Visibility checked at ingest and filtered again at query time
Redact PII and card numbers (Luhn-valid PANs) before the LLM call and before logging. Vendor under a DPA with no training on inputs
the bot answers only from public help-center articles. It does not read customer account data
Canary vs control: resolution, handoff, CSAT, cost per resolved conversation; reviewed transcript sample... content-gap reports go to the docs team
Hard caps: 4k input / 512 output tokens per turn, 5 turns per session, and a provider-account spend limit

traps.evidence: Every answer must be grounded in a cited article... Zero uncited commitments
Visibility checked at ingest and filtered again at query time
Prompt+RAG... Docs change often, so grounding beats baked-in knowledge
Eval report per index_version in CI artifacts... re-run every build
a simple fixed pipeline rather than an agent... One service, one ingestion worker, one Postgres with pgvector

note: An exemplary plan: grounded citations with executor-enforced handoff, retrieval-time visibility filtering, labeled eval gates and reversibility-aware decisions avoid all traps; only concrete cost estimation falls short of the top anchor.
